# Isotopic Fractionation as a Mechanistic Probe in Light-Driven C–H Bond Exchange Reactions

**Authors:** Guanqi Qiu; Chi-Li Ni; Robert R. Knowles

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

## Abstract

Here we report a diagnostic framework for elucidating the mechanisms of photoredox-based hydrogen isotope exchange (HIE) reactions based on hydrogen/deuterium (H/D) fractionation. Traditional thermal HIE methods generally proceed by reversible bond cleavage and bond reformation steps that share a common transition state. Yet, bond cleavage and bond reformation in light-driven HIE reactions can proceed via multiple, non-degenerate sets of elementary steps, complicating both mechanistic analysis and attendant optimization efforts. Building on classical treatments of equilibrium isotope effects, the fractionation method presented here extracts information regarding the nature of the key bond-forming and bond-breaking steps by comparing the extent of deuterium incorporation into an exchangeable C–H bond in the substrate relative to the H/D isotopic ratio of a solvent reservoir. We show that the extent of fractionation is sensitive to the mechanism of the exchange process and provides a means to distinguish between degenerate and non-degenerate mechanisms for isotopic exchange. In model systems, the mechanisms implied by the fractionation method align with those predicted by thermochemical considerations. We then employed the method to study HIE reactions whose mechanisms are ambiguous on thermodynamic grounds.

## Abstract

## Introduction

The scope of light-driven, radical-based C–H exchange reactions has expanded significantly in recent years with applications in isotopic labelling,1–6 selective epimerization,7–11 and deracemization reactions.12,13 As these exchange reactions proceed over multiple potential energy surfaces, the mechanisms of C–H bond cleavage and C–H bond reformation can proceed via distinct elementary steps.14,15 For example, C–H bond cleavage reactions that generate carbon-centered radicals can occur via either hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT)16,17 or by stepwise electron transfer/proton transfer (ETPT)18,19 pathways. Similarly, multiple mechanisms are possible to reform the C–H bond, as carbon-centered radicals can undergo either stepwise single-electron reduction to a carbanion intermediate20 followed by protonation or by reduction via HAT21 from an appropriate donor (Scheme 1a). Consequently, understanding which mechanisms are operative in a given exchange reaction is often non-trivial and can vary as a function of the substrates, catalysts, and reaction conditions. As knowledge of the operative mechanism is necessary for the selection of optimal conditions, methods that shed light on this question will be valuable additions to this burgeoning area of research.

To this end, we report here a diagnostic framework for studying the mechanism of photoredox hydrogen isotope exchange processes based on hydrogen/deuterium fractionation.22 H/D fractionation has been previously utilized for elucidating enzymatic reaction mechanisms23 while heavy-atom isotopic fractionation methods have seen use in geochemistry as paleotemperature probes.24 Our method extracts information regarding the nature of the bond-forming and bond-breaking steps by comparing the extent of deuterium incorporation into a C–H bond in the substrate relative to the H/D isotopic ratio of a protic solvent. As shown below, the extent of fractionation is sensitive to the mechanism of the exchange and provides insight into the nature of elementary steps involved.

## Results and Discussion

As a model for this study, we focused on light-driven isotopic exchange reactions wherein a C–H bond in the substrate continuously undergoes H/D exchange upon irradiation with blue light in the presence of an Ir-based photocatalyst, a thiol H-atom donor, and a Brønsted base in a solvent mixture comprised of varying molar ratios of CH3OH and CD3OD. For a given combination of substrate and catalysts, five separate light-driven isotopic exchange reactions are performed with five different molar ratios of CH3OH and CD3OD. The slope of the plot of the equilibrium [D-substrate]/[H-substrate] ratio versus the solvent [CD3OD]/[CH3OH] ratio is taken as the fractionation slope for a given reaction.

We hypothesized that the magnitude of this fractionation slope should vary as a function of the exchange mechanism (Scheme 1b). Our analysis expands on classical treatments of equilibrium isotope effects (EIEs) by taking into account the viability of non-degenerate exchange mechanisms wherein the bond-forming and bond-breaking events proceed via distinct elementary steps – a unique feature of these light-driven methods. To illustrate this, we first considered the limiting case where the exchange mechanism proceeds through reversible thiol-mediated HAT steps – abstraction of an H-atom from the substrate C–H/D bond by a thiyl radical, followed by C-radical reduction via HAT from the thiol S–H/D bond. When the system reaches equilibrium, the product isotopic ratio (C–H/D) will be proportional to the thiol isotopic ratio (S–H/D) and to a proportionality constant that is equal to the ratio of the kinetic isotope effects (KIE) for the C–H cleavage and C–H reformation steps (Figure 1a). As the C–H and S–H abstraction steps proceed through a common transition state, the zero-point energy difference (ΔZPE) for the transition structure will be identical in both the forward and reverse directions (Figure 1b), leading to the cancellation of this term in the resulting isotope effect expressions. In each reaction, the [S–D]/[S–H] ratio in the thiol HAT cocatalyst is taken to be equal to the ratio of [CD3OD]/[CH3OH] in the solvent.25 Consequently, for reversible HAT, a plot of substrate [C–D]/[C–H] versus [CD3OD]/[CH3OH] at equilibrium results in a linear correlation with e(ΔΔZPE/RT), where ΔΔZPE is the difference in zero-point energies between the C–H/C–D and S–H/S–D bonds, as in conventional EIE determinations. The slope of this linear correlation is the aforementioned fractionation slope. The requisite ΔΔZPE values can be readily determined computationally, with typical values of e(ΔΔZPE/RT) between 1.0 and 1.2 for exchange between C–H and S–H bonds (see Supporting Information for details).

An observed fractionation slope in good agreement with the predicted values of e(ΔΔZPE/RT) is consistent with a degenerate pathway for isotopic exchange.26 However, any significant deviation from this value is a clear indication that other non-degenerate mechanisms are operative in which the C–H/D cleavage and reformation proceed via distinct elementary steps. In these cases, the transition states for bond cleavage and bond formation are not identical. Each will have its own unique kinetic isotope effect, the ratio of which will determine the fractionation slope (Figure 1c). We show here that these slopes can vary significantly from those expected for degenerate pathways, providing insights into the elementary steps involved in a given HIE reaction or even when multiple mechanisms are operative simultaneously. Additionally, the fractionation slope also reflects potential changes in mechanism that can arise when certain catalytic components are omitted from the reaction.

To illustrate this idea, we studied the isotopic fractionation of six substrates using different combinations of Ir photocatalysts27–29 and thiol-based HAT catalysts, together with a common dialkyl phosphate base (Chart 1). The broad range of redox potentials and S–H bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) accessible in this set of catalysts enables us to access a variety of mechanistic regimes for both the bond-breaking and bond-forming steps of the exchange. Each entry in Table 1 reports the fractionation slope for the indicated substrate upon reaction with the indicated photocatalyst, thiol, and base, along with accompanying thermochemical values for the associated ET and HAT steps. For every entry in Table 1, 1H-NMR analysis revealed that reactions performed in pure CD3OD resulted in >95% deuterium incorporation at the indicated exchangeable site(s) with >90% yield.30 We verified that each of the H/D exchange reactions discussed here reaches equilibrium by approaching the equilibrium state from either pure D-labeled substrate or mixtures of H- and D-labeled substrates. Details are presented in the Supporting Information.

Entries 1 and 2 in Table 1 highlight that the exchange mechanism for a given substrate can be varied by simply changing the combination of photocatalyst and thiol HAT catalyst employed. The excited state of photocatalyst Ir-1 is not sufficiently oxidizing to engage in SET with the N-aryl urea substrate, precluding an oxidation-deprotonation pathway for C–H cleavage (entry 1). On the other hand, the S-H bond strength in thioacetic acid (S–H BDFE ~89 kcal/mol)21 is sufficiently low that thiyl radical formation via multisite proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) is feasible with the indicated Ir/phosphate catalyst pairs.31 The resulting thiyl radical can effectively engage in HAT with aliphatic C–H bonds in a wide range of compounds.32 We propose that under the given conditions, substrate deuteration takes place through a degenerate HAT/HAT mechanism. The photocatalyst and base activate the thiol S-H bond, producing a thiyl radical capable of extracting a hydrogen atom from the exchangeable C-H bond in the substrate. This results in a carbon-centered radical intermediate. A deuterium atom from the deuterated thiol is then transferred to the radical intermediate, yielding the deuterated form of the substrate. The comparable bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) of approximately 90 kcal/mol for both the urea C-H bond and the thioacetic acid S-H bond facilitate this reversible HAT processes. The resulting fractionation slope is 1.03, which is in good agreement with the theoretical value of 1.11 (Figure 2).

Switching from thioacetic acid to thiophenol (entry 2) still allows for the generation of thiyl radicals via PCET. However, the lower bond strength of the S–H bond in thiophenol (BDFE = 79 kcal/mol)33 renders H-atom abstraction from the urea C–H bond by the aryl thiyl prohibitively endergonic (ΔG° = +10 kcal/mol). This rationale was supported by the observation that under otherwise identical conditions to entry 1 in pure CD3OD, replacing thioacetic acid with thiophenol resulted in no observable deuterium incorporation. Alternatively, the excited state of photocatalyst Ir-2 is sufficiently oxidizing to remove an electron from the N-aryl urea substrate, enabling a stepwise oxidation-deprotonation pathway with the phosphate base to cleave the C–H bond. Reduction of the resulting carbon-centered radical via HAT from thiophenol is favorable (ΔG° = −10 kcal/mol), and therefore a likely mechanism for bond reformation. The experimental fractionation slope under these conditions is 0.39, significantly lower than the theoretical HAT/HAT fractionation slope of 1.12 (Figure 2). This value is consistent with an ETPT/HAT mechanism where the C–H bond cleavage and reformation proceed through distinct elementary steps. The same endpoint values for isotopic incorporation were also attained when using highly-deuterated forms of the starting material, supporting that the observed H/D ratios accurately reflect a dynamic stationary state. These results are consistent with the exclusive mechanistic proposal predicted by the thermochemical properties of the substrate and catalysts and serve to benchmark the framework developed here.

Encouraged by these results, we examined a series of substrates that, on the basis of simple thermodynamic arguments, are expected to undergo H/D exchange exclusively via degenerate HAT/HAT mechanisms. These substrates were chosen to have C–H BDFEs comparable to the thioacetic acid S–H bond and to have oxidation potentials that were inaccessible for SET with the excited state of Ir-3. The pyrrolidinone substrate has an experimental fractionation slope of 1.09, which is in excellent agreement with the theoretical value of 1.04 (entry 3). Abstraction from the ethereal C–H bond in 2,5-dimethyltetrahydrofuran by the thiyl radical derived from thioacetic acid is modestly endergonic (ΔG° = +3 kcal/mol), but still results in efficient deuterium incorporation (entry 4). The fractionation slope for this substrate is 1.00, again consistent with a degenerate HAT/HAT mechanism for isotopic exchange.

In entry 5, the unsymmetric diarylmethane substrate (Ep/2 = 1.23 V vs Fc+/Fc) cannot be oxidized by the excited state of Ir-1. However, its weak C–H bond34 can engage in HAT with the thiyl radical derived from thioacetic acid (ΔG° = −5 kcal/mol). The thermodynamic driving force for this HAT step renders the reverse HAT process unfavorable. Instead, the intermediate carbon-centered radical can be favorably reduced to its corresponding carbanion (E(C•/C–) ~ −1.8 V vs Fc+/Fc)35 by the reduced form of Ir-1 (E(IrIII/IrII) = −1.76 V vs Fc+/Fc) and protonated by solvent. Therefore, C–H bond reformation is expected to proceed via a stepwise ETPT process resulting in an overall mechanism of exchange by HAT/ETPT. The observed fractionation slope of 2.05, which is significantly higher than the theoretical value of 1.09 for the degenerate HAT/HAT pathway, is consistent with this proposal.

Notably, thioacetic acid is able to facilitate high degrees of deuterium incorporation via hydrogen-atom abstraction of C–H bonds in compounds difficult to oxidize directly by single-electron transfer (entries 3–5), indicating that it may prove more broadly useful in expanding the scope of substrates amenable to preparative hydrogen-isotope exchange reactions.

Entries 6 and 7 constitute another set of catalyst combinations that lead to different mechanisms for the same substrate. The excited state of photocatalyst Ir-4 cannot oxidize the N-aryl urea substrate, precluding an oxidation-deprotonation pathway. However, C–H abstraction by the thiyl radical derived from thioacetic acid is roughly thermoneutral, enabling reversible HAT. The experimental fractionation slope is 1.12, which is in excellent agreement with the calculated value of 1.11 (entry 6). Switching from thioacetic acid to thiophenol results in a significantly endergonic abstraction of the urea C–H bond, thus preventing an HAT-initiated mechanism (entry 7). Instead, using Ir-2 enables the oxidation-deprotonation pathway for C–H bond cleavage. Thus, an overall ETPT/HAT mechanism is expected. The experimental fractionation slope is 0.46, consistent with this hypothesis.

For entries 1–7, the exchange mechanism indicated by the fractionation slope can be predicted in advance on the basis of thermochemical considerations that strongly favor specific mechanisms. As illustrated in entries 8–11, this method can also be used to shed light on the operative reactivity modes for reactions where the mechanism is not clearly predicted on thermodynamic grounds. By employing both thioacetic acid and the strongly oxidizing Ir-2, we sought to determine the operative mechanism for C–H bond exchange in a scenario where multiple pathways are thermodynamically reasonable (entry 8). The experimental fractionation slope is 0.24, signifying that the ETPT/HAT mechanism is dominant over a potentially competitive HAT/HAT process. In entry 9, the excited state of photocatalyst Ir-4 can directly oxidize the aniline substrate, enabling access to an oxidation-deprotonation pathway for isotopic exchange. Simultaneously, the comparable BDFEs between the α-amino C–H bond36 and the thioacetic acid S–H bond also suggest that an HAT/HAT mechanism may be viable. The measured fractionation slope is 1.01, which is in fair agreement with the calculated value of 1.16. This value is consistent with a dominant HAT/HAT pathway, potentially in parallel with a minor ETPT/HAT pathway. Switching to the more oxidizing photocatalyst Ir-2 decreases the fractionation slope to 0.61 (entry 10) suggesting a mixed mechanism of ETPT/HAT and HAT/HAT. Subsequently increasing the thiol loading to 100 mol% results in a higher fractionation slope of 0.82 (entry 11). This is consistent with the same mixed mechanism as in entry 10 but with an increased percentage of the HAT/HAT pathway due to the increased favorability of thiol PCET activation.

The fractionation method discussed here can be applied to a variety of mechanistic scenarios beyond those previously mentioned. For instance, some recent studies have suggested that hydrogen isotope exchange can occur through non-degenerate HAT/HAT mechanisms. In these cases, two separate HAT catalysts mediate the bond formation and cleavage events. As a result, the forward and reverse hydrogen atom abstraction steps are no longer the microscopic reverse of one another, and the fractionation slope becomes equal to the ratio of the KIEs for each HAT event. Our method can help differentiate this mechanistic scenario from one where a single HAT catalyst is solely responsible for isotopic exchange. To demonstrate this, we analyzed a reaction recently reported by Wendlandt and colleagues, which focused on the epimerization of unactivated stereogenic methine C−H bonds (Scheme 2).37 In their original study, the epimerization process was proposed to proceed through a non-degenerate HAT-HAT mechanism facilitated by two distinct HAT catalysts: a photo-excited state of a decatungstate polyanion and 4-chlorothiophenol, which is generated in situ. This non-degenerate HAT/HAT process was proposed to be the exclusive mechanism for epimerization since alternative steps could be discounted on thermochemical grounds. We measured the fractionation slopes for this reaction, obtaining slopes of 0.47 and 0.44 for the two diastereomers, which represent the ratio of the KIEs for the two HAT events. If 4-chlorophenol was the only HAT catalyst responsible for isotopic exchange, the predicted fractionation slope could be calculated from e(ΔΔZPE/RT) and would be close to 1.1. Deviation from the slope predicted for a degenerate process provides additional support for a non-degenerate HAT/HAT mechanism. The agreement in mechanistic predictions indicates that our fractionation method can be useful for investigating the operative reactivity modes for C–H exchange reactions involving distinct HAT catalysts. This tool may be particularly useful when degenerate and non-degenerate HAT/HAT mechanisms cannot be clearly differentiated on the basis of thermodynamics alone.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, a simple method for isotopic fractionation is presented here as a useful diagnostic tool for probing the mechanisms of reversible C–H bond cleavage reactions in photoredox catalysis. This method relies on characteristic differences in the efficiency of deuterium incorporation for reactions wherein the C–H bond cleavage and reformation steps proceed via different elementary steps – a unique feature of excited-state redox-based methods. For reactions where two mechanisms are concurrently operative, the contributions of each mechanism to the overall exchange process can be estimated. This method also has applications in the optimization of photochemical deuteration schemes. As mechanisms with higher fractionation slopes incorporate deuterium from the solvent reservoir into the substrate more efficiently, choosing appropriate catalysts can also allow for more efficient deuteration reactions. We are optimistic that this method will provide useful insights and guidance for expanding the scope of other useful C–H exchange processes, including photocatalytic deracemization and epimerization methods.
